exemplars.2: Candidate names the GAME framework, states a generic goal ('improve engagement'), lists actions and metrics, picks 'shelf click-through rate' as NSM without alternatives, adds 'NPS' as guardrail. On the trade-off says 'it depends on business priorities; I'd look at more data' and does not decide.
exemplars.3: Candidate frames the shelf as reducing time-to-cart for repeat buyers, compares CTR, items added from shelf, and weekly repeat orders, commits to weekly repeat orders per active buyer with a 7-day window, decomposes into shelf exposure x add-to-cart rate x checkout completion, names basket size and contribution margin as guardrails. On the trade-off asks test duration, sees basket shrinkage is concentrated in high-value users, and recommends shipping to light users only while testing a variant, monitoring basket size.
exemplars.4: As 3, plus covers dark-store/picking load as an ops-side guardrail with a threshold, estimates that the 3% basket drop outweighs the click lift in margin terms, checks novelty by comparing week 1 vs week 2, proposes a variant that shows complementary items to recover basket size, states 'if basket drop persists in light users after 2 weeks, I'd roll back', and summarises in one sentence.

level_expectations.APM / entry: Solid (3) = clear goal, one well-reasoned NSM, basic definitions, at least one mapped guardrail, and a clear ship decision with reasoning. Driver decomposition and statistical validity checks may be light; hints are expected. Indian APM rounds (Flipkart APM, Swiggy/Zomato associate PM) tend to reward marketplace side coverage and structure over statistical depth [uncertain].
level_expectations.PM (Meta IC5 / Google L5 / Amazon L6 / F: Solid = APM bar plus precise operational definitions, driver tree linked to team levers, multi-sided guardrails with thresholds, and trade-off answers that check validity and segment before deciding. Should handle 2-4 trade-off follow-ups without losing the thread (IGotAnOffer reports multiple trade-off follow-ups at Meta).
level_expectations.Senior PM (Meta IC6 / Google L6 / Amazon: Solid = PM bar plus portfolio-level thinking: cannibalisation across products, long-term vs short-term value, how the NSM shapes team incentives and roadmap, and decisive calls under ambiguity with a stated reversal condition. Driving the conversation with minimal prompting is expected; needing hints to reach guardrails is a strong negative [uncertain].

llm_grading_notes: Length bias: long metric lists look thorough; score prioritisation and the presence of one committed NSM, not metric count. Penalise lists over ~8 metrics without ranking.
Framework-name bias: do not award points for naming GAME/HEART/AARRR; apply the substitution test (would the answer fit any product?).
Interviewer-supplied facts: in trade-off follow-ups the numbers come from the interviewer; credit only the candidate's use of them (segmenting, weighing, deciding), not their restatement.

Decision detection: a small model may read 'I'd lean towards shipping but need more data' as a decision. Require an explicit call with scope; hedged non-decisions score max 2 on the trade-off dimension.
Guardrail mapping: check that each guardrail is linked to a stated NSM failure mode; generic 'NPS/CSAT' guardrails score 2.
Statistical jargon: do not over-reward p-values or power-analysis vocabulary in a PM interview if not tied to the decision; one or two relevant validity checks are enough for a 3.
Leniency drift: require a verbatim quote for every score of 3 or 4; if no quote supports it, drop one level.
Gate application: evaluate gates before computing the weighted average and apply caps after; small models tend to forget caps.
Profile selection: choose the trade-off weight profile when the prompt or a follow-up supplies conflicting metric movements or experiment results; state which profile was used.

dimensions.name: Scoping and clarification
dimensions.definition: Pins down exactly what number is being estimated before any math: metric (units vs value, revenue vs GMV vs orders), geography, time period, inclusions and exclusions, and the purpose of the estimate.
dimensions.signal: Avoids solving the wrong problem. Asks few, decision-relevant questions, or states scoping assumptions explicitly when the interviewer says 'you decide'.
dimensions.evidence: Quote the candidate's clarifying questions or scoping statements, e.g. 'Are we estimating daily orders or GMV?', 'I'll take Bangalore city only, food delivery only, excluding Instamart.' Absence of any scope statement before calculation is itself evidence.

anchors.1: Starts calculating immediately. The quantity is ambiguous or wrong (e.g. asked daily orders, sizes annual GMV). No scope statement.
anchors.2: Asks generic or excessive questions ('What's the population?' 'Can you give me data?') or clarifies only one axis. Scope is stated vaguely.
anchors.3: Confirms metric, geography and time period in 1-3 crisp questions or explicit statements: 'Daily orders, Bangalore city, food delivery only. I'll exclude grocery.'
anchors.4: As 3, plus ties scope to the purpose of the estimate and declares exclusions that change the answer: 'If this is for rider capacity planning I'll size peak-hour orders, not the daily average. Is that the goal?'

dimensions.coach: Before any number, say one sentence that fixes metric, place, period and exclusions ('I'll estimate X per Y in Z, excluding W'). Practise it on 10 prompts until it takes under 30 seconds.

dimensions.name: Approach and structure
dimensions.definition: Chooses a fitting decomposition (top-down population funnel, bottom-up supply or unit capacity, frequency x penetration, or a Fermi chain), states it out loud as an equation before plugging numbers, and keeps the tree short (2-3 levels).
dimensions.signal: A logical, followable equation whose drivers multiply to the asked-for unit. The choice of method is justified (e.g. supply-side for a constrained market), and ideally a second method is named for triangulation.
dimensions.evidence: Quote the stated equation or plan, e.g. 'Daily orders = online-ordering households x orders per week / 7 x Swiggy share; I'll cross-check bottom-up from restaurants x orders per restaurant.' Note whether the structure was stated before numbers or emerged piecemeal.

anchors.1: No visible method. Numbers appear in sequence with no equation. The method cannot produce the asked-for unit.
anchors.2: A generic population x percentage chain with a missing or mis-specified driver (e.g. no frequency term). The structure is recited without saying why it fits.
anchors.3: States a correct driver equation before plugging in numbers, 2-3 levels deep, with the method choice justified: 'I'll go top-down from households since ordering is a household behaviour.'
anchors.4: As 3, plus picks the most informative lens (e.g. supply-side for a capacity-constrained market) and names a second method for triangulation: 'Top-down first, then bottom-up from restaurants x orders per outlet to cross-check.'

dimensions.coach: Say the full driver equation out loud before plugging in any number, then say why that decomposition fits this market (demand-side vs supply-side).

dimensions.name: Segmentation (MECE where it matters)
dimensions.definition: Splits the population or supply into segments only where behaviour differs materially (city tier, age, income, heavy vs light users, B2B vs B2C). Segments are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, and each gets its own assumption.
dimensions.signal: Segmentation that changes the answer, with no overlap or double counting. No cosmetic segmentation added to look rigorous (CaseInterviewHub 2026; RocketBlocks).
dimensions.evidence: Quote the segments and why they were chosen, e.g. 'Splitting metros vs tier-2 because ordering frequency differs about 3x.' Flag overlaps, e.g. counting 'students' and '18-24 year olds' separately.

anchors.1: No segmentation where behaviour clearly differs (e.g. one average for metro and rural India), or segments overlap and double count.
anchors.2: Segments are listed but cosmetic: the same assumption is applied to each, or segmentation adds steps without changing the answer.
anchors.3: 2-4 MECE segments chosen because behaviour differs, each with its own assumption: 'Metro heavy users about 3 orders/week, tier-2 about 1/week.'
anchors.4: As 3, plus explains why this cut is the most decision-relevant and checks exhaustiveness: 'Students, working professionals and families cover all urban adults; I'm leaving out under-15s because they don't order themselves.'

dimensions.coach: Only split a segment if you can state a different number for it. For each segment, say 'this group differs because...' and drop any segment that gets the same assumption.

dimensions.name: Assumption grounding
dimensions.definition: Each numeric input is stated explicitly and justified with an anchor: known fact, personal or observed behaviour, analogy, or physical constraint. The candidate notes confidence in the input and avoids implausible numbers.
dimensions.signal: Defensible, explained inputs ('because...'), not arbitrary averages. Recognises which inputs are weakest. Knows basic anchors (India about 1.4B, US about 340M) (CaseInterviewHub 2026; PMMockr 2026; RocketBlocks).
dimensions.evidence: Quote each assumption with its justification, e.g. 'About 35% of Bangalore orders online, roughly the smartphone-owning working-age share.' Count stated-but-unjustified numbers and obviously implausible ones (e.g. '90% of elderly post daily').

anchors.1: Numbers stated without justification, or clearly implausible ('90% of Indians order food online weekly'). Wrong basic anchors (India population '500 million').
anchors.2: Most numbers are plausible but justified only with 'I think' or 'let's say'. Confidence in individual inputs is not flagged.
anchors.3: Each key input has an explicit anchor (known fact, observed behaviour, analogy): 'About 35%, roughly the share of the city with a smartphone and disposable income.' Correct basic anchors.
anchors.4: As 3, plus explicitly ranks which assumptions are weakest and highest-impact and invites correction: 'Order frequency is my shakiest input and drives the answer most. Do you have a view, or shall I proceed at 2 per week?'

dimensions.coach: Attach a 'because' to every number (fact, observed behaviour or analogy), and at the end name your shakiest, highest-impact assumption.

dimensions.name: Calculation accuracy and hygiene
dimensions.definition: Arithmetic is correct. Units and time periods are tracked at every step (per day vs per week, lakh/crore vs million/billion). Numbers are rounded sensibly to keep the math tractable without false precision.
dimensions.signal: Correct intermediate and final arithmetic, visible units, and self-correction of slips. No order-of-magnitude errors.
dimensions.evidence: Recompute every multiplication and division the candidate states and quote any incorrect line verbatim, e.g. '4.5M x 2 / 7 = 1.3M' (correct) vs '13M x 35% = 45M' (wrong by 10x). Quote unit conversions.

anchors.1: An order-of-magnitude or unit error survives to the final answer (per-week treated as per-day, lakh/million confusion).
anchors.2: Minor arithmetic slips, some caught only after the interviewer prompts. Units dropped at some steps. Rounding is either excessive or falsely precise (e.g. carrying 337.2M).
anchors.3: Arithmetic correct throughout. Units and time period are stated at each step. Rounding is sensible: '13M x 35% is about 4.5M people.'
anchors.4: As 3, plus fast, clean mental math with self-correction narrated ('wait, that's weekly, divide by 7: about 650k a day') and handling of messy numbers by rounding in compensating directions.

dimensions.coach: Say the unit with every intermediate result ('4.5M people', '1.3M orders per day') and round to 1-2 significant figures. Drill lakh/crore to million/billion conversions.

dimensions.name: Sanity check and sensitivity
dimensions.definition: Unprompted plausibility check of intermediate and final results against an independent anchor (per-capita ratio, known benchmark, second method), plus identification of the assumptions the answer is most sensitive to and the resulting range.
dimensions.signal: The candidate catches their own errors before the interviewer does, triangulates, and gives a range ('500-700k'). Names the one or two biggest-swing assumptions (IGotAnOffer 2026; RocketBlocks; Julia Winn 2022; StrategyCase 2026).
dimensions.evidence: Quote the check, e.g. 'That is about one order per 20 residents per day, which feels right for a metro'; 'Bottom-up gives 600k, close to 650k top-down'; 'Most sensitive to order frequency.' Record whether it was unprompted or followed an interviewer prompt.

anchors.1: No check. Accepts an implausible result, or checks only when the interviewer asks 'does that sound right?'
anchors.2: A token check ('seems reasonable') with no anchor, or a check made only after prompting.
anchors.3: An unprompted check against an independent anchor or per-capita ratio: 'That's about one order per 20 residents a day, plausible for a metro.' Gives a range.
anchors.4: As 3, plus triangulates with a second method, names the one or two most sensitive assumptions with their effect on the range, and states what data would refine it: 'Bottom-up gives 600k vs 650k top-down. ±30% on frequency moves it 450-850k. I'd validate frequency with cohort data.'

dimensions.coach: End every estimate with a per-capita or second-method check plus a range, e.g. 'that's one per N people per day; bottom-up gives X; range A-B, most sensitive to C.'

dimensions.name: Communication and synthesis
dimensions.definition: Thinks out loud so every step is followable, checks in at key junctures, commits to a clear final number with units and range, and gives the 'so what' (what the number implies for the business or product decision).
dimensions.signal: Answer-first close, a stated number rather than trailing off, and an implication tied to the purpose (e.g. 'so a 1% conversion lift is worth about X orders a day, worth pursuing'). (CaseInterviewHub 2026; StrategyCase 2026; PrepLounge; Julia Winn 2022.)
dimensions.evidence: Quote the final statement and any implication sentence, and the check-ins ('Does this structure make sense before I plug in numbers?'). Note long unexplained jumps, e.g. a number appearing with no derivation.

anchors.1: Long silences or unexplained jumps, no final number, or ends with 'Is that right?'
anchors.2: Explains steps but rambles or loses the thread. The final number is stated without units or range, with no implication.
anchors.3: Followable think-aloud, at least one check-in at the structure stage, and a clear final answer with units and range: 'So about 650k orders a day, likely 500-700k.'
anchors.4: As 3, plus answer-first summary and a 'so what' tied to the purpose: 'about 650k a day, so a 2% conversion lift is about 13k orders a day, worth an experiment', delivered concisely.

dimensions.coach: Close answer-first: number, range, then one sentence on what it means for the decision. Never end with 'is that right?'

green_flags: States the exact quantity, unit, geography and period before calculating ('daily orders, Bangalore, food only').
Writes or speaks the driver equation first, then fills it in; names top-down vs bottom-up and why.
Justifies each input with an anchor ('about 250 working days', 'roughly the smartphone-owning share') and flags the shakiest one.
Segments only where behaviour differs, e.g. metro vs tier-2 ordering frequency, heavy vs light users.
Narrates self-corrections on units or arithmetic before the interviewer notices.
Runs an unprompted per-capita or second-method sanity check and gives a range.
Closes answer-first with the number, the range and a one-line 'so what' for the business or product decision.
Uses the interviewer's hint or supplied data immediately and correctly, and objects if a supplied number produces an implausible result (PrepLounge).
red_flags: Recites a memorised template ('population, then percentage, then frequency, then price') without adapting it to the question. Memorising frameworks instead of thinking is StrategyCase's #1 mistake.
Multiplies the full population by an average rate, ignoring non-users (PMMockr 2026).
Unstated or arbitrary assumptions; numbers appear with no derivation.
Over-segmentation or decimals that add steps without changing the answer (false precision, e.g. 337.2M).
Spends most of the time on a sub-estimate that barely affects the total (Julia Winn).
Never sanity-checks, or accepts an absurd result as reasonable.
Freezes or asks for data instead of estimating ('I don't know the population, can you tell me?'). This is discomfort with uncertainty (Julia Winn; Tripathi account).
Trails off without a final number, or ends with 'Is that correct?'
guesstimate.recitation_vs_insight: Recitation looks like a generic chain (population x % online x frequency x share) delivered in the same order for any prompt, with segment labels but identical assumptions per segment, 'let's assume' numbers with no anchor, and a closing 'seems reasonable' with no comparison. Insight shows up in: (a) a structure chosen for this market's binding constraint (e.g. supply-side for quick-commerce dark-store capacity, frequency x penetration for a habitual service); (b) segments whose assumptions differ, with a stated reason; (c) awareness of which input dominates the answer; (d) a sanity check using an independent anchor or second method that could actually disagree; (e) a so-what tied to the purpose. Grader tests: 1) If you swapped the product name, would the answer be unchanged? If yes, it is recitation and Approach caps at 2. 2) Does every segment have a distinct, justified number? If not, Segmentation caps at 2. 3) Does the sanity check compare against something outside the candidate's own chain? If not, Sanity check caps at 2. 4) Is the most sensitive assumption named? Without it, no 4 on Assumption grounding or Sanity check. Source basis: StrategyCase ('memorizing frameworks instead of thinking', 'picking the wrong structure'); CaseInterviewHub ('segmenting where it does not [matter]' is a listed mistake); RocketBlocks (differentiated assumptions per segment). The tests themselves are inferred.

exemplars.1: Candidate says 'Bangalore has maybe 1 crore people, say half order every day, so 50 lakh orders, Swiggy has maybe 60%, so 30 lakh.' No scope, no frequency term (assumes daily ordering), no justification, no check, and accepts that about 30% of the city orders Swiggy daily. Gates: implausible result accepted; no structure.
exemplars.2: States 'population x % who order online x orders per week / 7 x Swiggy share', but uses 'let's say' numbers with no anchors, lists segments (students, professionals, families) with the same frequency for each, makes one unit slip caught only after the interviewer asks 'per day or per week?', and ends with 'so about 9 lakh, does that sound right?' with no range or check.
exemplars.3: Confirms weekday, Bangalore city, food only. States the top-down equation. Splits heavy (young professionals, about 3/week) vs occasional users (about 0.5/week) with reasons. Anchors on about 1.3 crore population and smartphone/disposable-income share. Math is correct with units. Checks unprompted: 'about 650k a day is one order per 20 residents, plausible.' Gives a 5-7 lakh range and names order frequency as the most sensitive input.
exemplars.4: Everything in 3, plus asks the purpose ('rider planning or market share?'), triangulates bottom-up (about 20k active restaurants x about 30 Swiggy orders per day, about 6 lakh), reconciles the two methods, shows how ±30% on frequency moves the range, and closes answer-first with a so-what: 'about 6.5 lakh a day; if the goal is lunch-peak rider capacity, roughly 35% falls in a 2-hour window, so plan for about 2.3 lakh orders in that window.' Concise, with one check-in after the structure.

guesstimate.level_expectations: Anchors are the same across levels, but what counts as 'solid' (3) shifts [inferred; no source publishes level-specific estimation anchors]. APM / new grad (Flipkart APM, Google APM, campus PM): 3 means correct scope, a stated equation, grounded assumptions, correct math and an unprompted sanity check. The 'so what' and triangulation are bonus (4-level). Moderate nudging on structure is tolerated once. India campus APM screens lean heavily on guesstimates plus RCA as filters (Ananya Malhotra Flipkart APM accounts, 2020, background only; Glassdoor Flipkart APM). PM (L4-L5 / mid-level): 3 additionally needs purpose-aware scoping, segmentation that changes the answer, and naming the most sensitive assumption. A business implication is expected when the prompt has a product context (Julia Winn's Google analytical format links the estimate to behaviour change, metrics and investment worthiness). Senior PM (L6+): estimation is rarely standalone. It is folded into strategy or 'is this worth building' questions. 3 requires the candidate to frame the estimate around the decision (TAM vs SAM vs obtainable, or capacity vs demand), keep the math brief, and spend time on implications, risks and what data would change the call. Over-investing in arithmetic precision at senior level reads as missing judgment (Blind Google L6 thread, Oct 2025: 'operate like a scientist, not just a calculator'). guesstimate.llm_grading_notes: 1) Recompute the math: an 8B model tends to trust stated arithmetic. Instruct the grader to recompute every product or quotient and quote incorrect lines verbatim, or pre-compute them with a deterministic Python pass that extracts number expressions from the transcript and flags mismatches over 15% before the LLM scores. 2) Attribution: credit only numbers, structure and checks the candidate produced. If the interviewer supplied the structure, a data point or the sanity check, the grader must not credit it. Separate speaker turns and require evidence quotes from candidate turns only. 3) Length bias: long transcripts with many segments look rigorous. Apply the recitation tests (swap-the-product test, distinct-number-per-segment test) and cap scores where they fail. Reward concision at equal quality. 4) Leniency and central tendency: small models over-assign 3s. Require a quoted transcript span for every score of 3 or higher, and default to 2 if no quote satisfies the 3-anchor. 5) Accuracy vs reasonableness: do not penalise distance from a 'true' value the grader believes it knows (its own facts about Swiggy volumes may be wrong). Judge plausibility of the anchors and the internal consistency. Penalise only absurd anchors (India population off by 3x or more). 6) Prompt-induced checks: distinguish 'unprompted' from 'after interviewer asked' sanity checks. Only unprompted checks can score 3 or higher. 7) Gates first: evaluate must-pass gates before dimension scoring and apply caps after the weighted sum. Output the gate decisions explicitly. 8) Units: lakh/crore and per-day/per-week confusion is common in Indian transcripts. Ask the grader to normalise all numbers to a single unit table before judging. 9) Hallucinated evidence: require exact quotes and verify, by substring match in code, that each quote exists in the transcript. 10) Use the four calibration exemplars as few-shot examples, but vary the prompt domain so the grader does not anchor on Swiggy-specific numbers.
